opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to the fact that the real value of a model like AlphaFold 3 isn't realized by us alone. It's realized when thousands of scientists around the world put it to work on their own questions, questions we'd never think to ask ourselves. We saw that with AlphaFold 2. Once it was out there, researchers used it in ways we never anticipated, from studying neglected diseases to designing enzymes to understanding basic biology in organisms nobody had looked at closely before. That kind of breadth only happens when access is easy and free.

Academic labs are often where the most curiosity-driven, foundational work happens, and they're also often the most resource-constrained. If you put a powerful tool behind a paywall, you end up concentrating it in the hands of the people who already have the most resources. Making it freely available to academics levels that playing field a bit. A grad student somewhere with a laptop and a hypothesis can now get a structural prediction for a protein-ligand complex or a protein-DNA interaction in minutes, something that might otherwise take months of experimental work, if it were possible at all.

There's also a feedback loop that matters to us. When the scientific community uses the model, they stress-test it. They find where it works brilliantly and where it falls down, and that tells us a lot about what to build next. So it's good for science broadly, but it also makes our own work better.

And honestly, it's a big part of why many of us got into this in the first place. The goal was always to accelerate scientific discovery, and you can't do that if the tool sits on a shelf.

r001.rationale: The response connects AlphaFold 3’s value to scientists using it for their own questions, then cites understanding basic biology as a use of AlphaFold models beyond other applications.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it comes down to what you want the model to actually do in the world. AlphaFold 2 was a bit of a watershed moment for us, and part of why it had the impact it did is that we released it fully, with the weights, and the academic community just ran with it. We saw millions of researchers using it, people using it in ways we'd never anticipated, in fields that had nothing to do with what we were originally thinking about. That kind of distributed exploration is something no single lab, Isomorphic included, could ever do on its own.

So with AlphaFold 3 the model is more powerful. It's not just proteins anymore, it's proteins with ligands, with nucleic acids, with ions, with modifications, essentially the whole molecular world that a cell is made of. And the number of scientific questions that opens up is enormous. If you're an academic studying some obscure pathway or some rare disease that's never going to be commercially interesting, you should be able to pick up this tool and use it. That's where a lot of the fundamental understanding comes from, and honestly, that's where a lot of our own ideas get sharpened, because the community pushes on the model, finds where it breaks, and tells us.

There's also just a basic philosophy to it. This work was built on decades of publicly funded structural biology, on the PDB, on people depositing their experimental structures for everyone to use. It would feel wrong to take all of that and then wall off the result. Giving academics free access is partly about accelerating science, and partly about honouring the ecosystem that made the thing possible in the first place.

And from Isomorphic's side, the commercial drug discovery work is a different problem. We're using these models in an integrated way, with chemists and biologists, on specific programmes. Free academic access doesn't take away from that at all. If anything, a healthier, faster-moving scientific community makes everything we do easier.

r001.rationale: The response says AlphaFold 3 can help academics study obscure pathways and rare diseases, contributing to fundamental understanding, and distinguishes that scientific use from commercial drug discovery.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s important because the value of a tool like AlphaFold 3 ultimately comes from what people can do with it. There are researchers all over the world with deep expertise in a particular disease or biological question who don’t necessarily have the resources to build these models themselves. Free academic access lowers that barrier and lets them explore questions they might otherwise struggle to tackle.

And these predictions are a starting point for experiments. If you can help a researcher develop a better hypothesis, decide which experiment to run, or interpret a result, you can accelerate that scientific process. Opening access means far more people can contribute their ideas—and those ideas are often where the unexpected discoveries come from.

r001.rationale: The response describes helping researchers investigate biological questions and guide experiments, but it does not state that AlphaFold 3 supports fundamental understanding of biology beyond drug design.

sol-6.1.text: I think the important thing is getting these tools into the hands of the scientists who can really use them. Predicting a molecular structure is a starting point: researchers still need to ask the right biological questions, design experiments, and test what the model suggests. Free academic access lowers the barrier to that work. It allows more people, across a much wider range of research areas, to explore ideas—and that gives us a better chance of turning advances in AI into useful scientific discoveries.

r001.rationale: The response mentions biological questions and research across a wide range of areas, but does not clearly state that AlphaFold 3 advances fundamental biological understanding beyond drug design.
